title: Substantiation cannot be an afterthought in nutraceutical advertising: ASCI CEO
summary: Advertising Standards Council of India review of nutraceutical advertisements has flagged widespread gaps in the substantiation of health claims, from promises to reverse PCOD and cleanse lungs to claims around blood sugar control and weight loss. In an...

contentHtml:
Mumbai: With growing awareness around preventive healthcare, nutrition and lifestyle-related conditions, consumers are increasingly turning to nutraceuticals and dietary supplements.The growing consumer demand is expected to drive India's nutritional supplements market from $22.94 billion in 2025 to $58.82 billion by 2034, according to estimates by market research firm IMARC.

However, as the market grows and matures, the advertising around it is also growing more ambitious.Brands are moving beyond broad wellness claims to promise specific health outcomes, with some even positioning supplements as alternatives to prescription therapies or claiming to reverse medical conditions.

Advt

In a recent review, the Advertising Standards Council of India (ASCI) flagged recurring concerns around the substantiation of health and wellness claims in nutraceutical advertisements. It evaluated 61 ads in the sector, out of which 60 were found to be in violation of the ASCI Code. One was still under review.

In an exclusive interaction with ETHealthworld, Manisha Kapoor, CEO, ASCI discusses how advertising claims in the sector have evolved, the growing challenges of monitoring digital promotions and why scientific evidence must precede, rather than follow, the marketing of health products.How has nutraceutical advertising changed in recent years? Are brands increasingly positioning supplements as solutions for specific medical conditions rather than products supporting general health and wellness?

Nutraceutical or supplement advertising has changed from being about generic claims around energy, immunity or wellbeing. We now see more specialised and specific claims. Our latest review looked at claims around weight management, skincare, anti-ageing, respiratory health and those that edged into treating specific conditions such as asthma, blood pressure, cholesterol and PCOS, including one wellness product that promised to “reverse PCOD”.

The promises have also become more deadline-oriented. Examples are “Lose 6 kgs in 60 days” and “Your thigh fat will be gone in 12 weeks” which come with before-and-after visuals. Some supplements now position themselves as alternatives to prescription therapies for chronic weight management and Type 2 diabetes. That puts them in territory where consumers may be making decisions about their medical care based on these claims.

Advt

Nutraceutical purchases are becoming more routine among consumers. An imarc study found that India’s nutritional supplements market is poised to increase from $22.94 billion in 2025 to $58.82 billion by 2034, growing at a CAGR of 10.70 per cent.As consumers become more health oriented, such supplements may be taken as lifestyle choices rather than after medical advice. Hence, any overstatement of claims or omission of information may cause incorrect intake and consequent health problems.Which nutraceutical categories and health claims are currently most concerning from an advertising standards perspective?

Advt

There are a few that stand out. In weight loss, there are time-bound promises, dramatic visuals and claims of being safer than established therapies.When it comes to blood sugar and metabolism, there are claims about curbing cravings and controlling post-meal sugar spikes, where the line with prescription treatment blurs.For skincare and anti-ageing, there are claims such as “Your skin, but 7 years younger” and “300% stronger skin defence against UV damage”. Glutathione ads also tied sun protection and de-tanning to visuals of darker skin turning lighter, which suggests skin lightening and reinforces a preference for lighter skin. One oral spray claimed three sprays gave three times faster absorption and reversed wrinkles.

In respiratory health, “lung cleansing” claims, black-to-pink lung visuals, and suggestions that a supplement can reverse the effects of smoking or pollution were observed.All of these were not substantiated with scientific evidence.ASCI has flagged misleading claims in nutraceutical advertising across multiple reviews and enforcement exercises. What recurring patterns have you observed over the years? Has the nature of misleading claims evolved as the market has expanded?Advertisers often can’t produce adequate clinical evidence or independent test reports showing the finished product delivers the advertised benefit. Words like “faster”, “more effective” and “first” are used without saying what the comparison is against. Promises are made before the evidence exists or based on very thin evidence rather than robust scientific data or trials.Often, the benefits of the ingredients are implied as those of the finished product. These could be very different from what the finished product can deliver.What is changing is how persuasive the claims have become. Visuals now carry much of the message, whether before-and-after images such as lungs turning pink from black. Claims have moved from general benefits to outcomes in fixed timeframes, references to new mechanisms like faster absorption through a new consumption method. Assessing these means looking at the overall impression created by words, visuals and promised outcomes together.In a recent review, ASCI found violations in all 60 completed nutraceutical advertising cases. Does this indicate a systemic problem with how the industry markets these products, rather than isolated instances of misleading advertising?We reviewed 61 ads and all needed modification; 29 were modified or withdrawn without contest, while 31 were found in violation of the ASCI code. One ad was under process.While it’s unfair to say this is a measure of the whole industry, the consistency is a concern. None of the advertisers who contested the complaints could provide adequate evidence for their claims, and many chose to withdraw or modify rather than defend them. That suggests substantiation is often treated as something to sort out after a complaint, not before the ad goes out.Many of the brands we examined belonged to new age D2C (direct-to-consumer) companies, who may be under intense pressure to show quick results. They are likely not to have full-fledged compliance or regulatory teams. Due to these reasons, we see a proliferation of half-truths and misleading claims. However, there would also be brands that are careful about communicating to their audiences in more trustworthy ways, and making their claims only after a thorough assessment of the evidence.How often do brands use ingredient-level research to substantiate claims about finished products? What scientific evidence should advertisers be expected to produce before making efficacy claims about a formulation? Where should the evidentiary threshold lie?This was a recurring issue in the cases we examined. The reasoning goes like this an ingredient has been studied for a benefit, so the product is assumed to deliver it. But a well-researched ingredient doesn’t establish that a finished formulation works. Dose, combination and form all matter.Our expectation is that the strength of the claim must match the strength of the evidence, and significant health claims need evidence specific to the product and the dose. In practice, that means clinical evidence or independent test reports on the product as marketed. The more a claim sounds like treatment, or promises a specific result in a specific time, the higher the bar. Superiority claims need to show what the product is better than and demonstrate that the advantage is real.How has the shift towards influencer-led marketing, social media and direct-to-consumer advertising changed the challenge of monitoring nutraceutical claims? How does ASCI hold brands, influencers and endorsers accountable when misleading health claims are promoted?The volume, speed and fragmentation of digital content make monitoring harder. A claim can go live, reach millions and disappear before a traditional review cycle catches it.On accountability, ASCI’s guidelines for influencer advertising in digital media require clear disclosure of material connections and expect influencers to do due diligence on the claims they make.The guidelines also make clear that, for posts related to health and nutrition, the influencer must have relevant qualifications such as a medical degree, or be a certified nurse, nutritionist, dietician, physiotherapist, psychologist, etc, depending on the specific advice being given.The influencer must disclose such qualifications and registration/certification details prominently.The Department of Consumer Affairs too has issued extensive guidelines on this matter. Celebrities, influencers and virtual influencers presenting themselves as health experts or medical practitioners, when sharing information, promoting products or services or making any health-related claims, must provide clear disclaimers, ensuring the audience understands that their endorsements are not seen as a substitute for professional medical advice, diagnosis or treatment.Endorsers are also encouraged to conduct a thorough review and ensure they are in a position to substantiate the claims made in the advertisement before endorsing a product or service.Responsibility sits with the brand and the influencer, and we address both. When a complaint is upheld, we ask for the ad to be modified or withdrawn, and non-compliant ads and repeat cases can be escalated to the relevant regulators, such as the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting or the Ministry of Ayush.Given that ASCI operates through a self-regulatory framework, how effective is it in deterring misleading advertising in a category that directly influences consumer health decisions?Self-regulation gives us agility and a frontline protection to consumers. This comes at no cost to the tax payers. Our average turnaround time for complaints is 15 days this financial year. ASCI also enjoys a high voluntary compliance rate in FY 2025-26, we had 86 per cent voluntary compliance. TV and print compliance stood at 97 per cent.Of the cases in the nutraceutical advertising sweep, advertisers modified or withdrew ads in 29 cases without contest, and the ones who contested could not substantiate their claims. That is quick correction at scale, done with a robust process at quick turnaround times.Repeat and wilful violators get escalated for full investigation to the relevant authority under statutory provisions.So, self-regulation and law work best together. We handle high-volume, fast-moving cases, and the statutory bodies have the legal authority to act where claims are serious or advertisers persist.How closely does ASCI coordinate with FSSAI and the Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) on misleading nutraceutical claims? Are there gaps in the existing regulatory framework that make it difficult to hold advertisers accountable?ASCI works with FSSAI and the CCPA, referring repeat and wilful offenders to them when it comes to cases that fall within their remit.The challenge lies in the fact that, while nutraceuticals are regulated by the FSSAI and are therefore technically considered food, many of these products are advertised as therapeutic. Regulation has been evolving and will need to evolve further as nutraceutical products get increasingly popular.Looking ahead, what changes are needed to improve accountability and consumer protection in nutraceutical advertising? Should there be stricter requirements for scientific substantiation, greater scrutiny of high-risk health claims or stronger monitoring of digital advertising?Advertisers should adopt an evidence-first policy. They should have product-specific, dose-specific substantiation before a claim goes live. Evidence shouldn’t be something put together after a complaint arrives.This is especially true when it comes to high-risk claims such as weight loss, blood sugar management, respiratory health and anything implying treatment.More attention needs to be paid to visuals and their overall impression. Before-and-after images, timelines and implied comparisons often make the promise more than the copy does, and they need the same scrutiny.For brands, this is also the sensible business choice. In a category where consumers are making decisions about their health, evidence is the foundation of trust. When it’s missing, trust erodes for the whole category.Often, an ingredient’s benefits are sought to be passed off as the benefit of the product. However, a beneficial ingredient doesn’t automatically mean that a finished formulation is effective. The claim must match the evidence furnished about the product.
